problem_text:
We have an undirected graph with 4 vertices (numbered 0..3) and 4 edges:
  edges = (0,2), (1,2), (1,3), (2,3)

Each vertex must receive one of 3 colors (0, 1, 2).
Color code per vertex v (2 qubits): low bit b0 = problem_qubits[2v], high bit b1 = problem_qubits[2v+1]; code value c = b0 + 2*b1.
Decoding is SURJECTIVE: c=0 (binary 00) -> color 0, c=1 (01) -> color 1, c=2 (10) -> color 2, and c=3 (binary 11) ALSO decodes to color 0.
All 2-bit codes are legal; there is no invalid code.
Worked example with the 11 code: if vertex 0 has code 11 and vertex 1 has code 00, both decode to color 0, so an edge (0,1) would be monochromatic and the constraint 'colors differ' is VIOLATED.

The classical predicate is f(x) = 1 if and only if, after decoding every vertex's 2-bit code to its color, every edge connects two vertices of DIFFERENT colors.

The partially filled grid is (rows top to bottom, '.' = free cell):
  . . 2
  1 2 0
  2 0 1

The free cells, in order, are (row, col): (0,0), (0,1).  Free cell number j is the j-th in this list.
Cell value code (2 qubits per free cell): free cell number j uses low bit b0 = problem_qubits[2j] and high bit b1 = problem_qubits[2j+1]; code c = b0 + 2*b1.
Decoding is SURJECTIVE: 00 -> value 0, 01 -> value 1, 10 -> value 2, and 11 ALSO decodes to value 0.  All codes are legal.
Worked example with the 11 code: if a free cell has code 11 it holds value 0; placing it in a row that already contains a given 0 VIOLATES the all-different constraint.

The classical predicate is f(x) = 1 if and only if decoding all free cells yields a completed grid that is a valid Latin square.

The partially filled grid is (rows top to bottom, '.' = free cell):
  1 . 2
  2 1 0
  . 2 .

The free cells, in order, are (row, col): (0,1), (2,0), (2,2).  Free cell number j is the j-th in this list.
Cell value code (2 qubits per free cell): free cell number j uses low bit b0 = problem_qubits[2j] and high bit b1 = problem_qubits[2j+1]; code c = b0 + 2*b1.
Decoding is SURJECTIVE: 00 -> value 0, 01 -> value 1, 10 -> value 2, and 11 ALSO decodes to value 0.  All codes are legal.
Worked example with the 11 code: if a free cell has code 11 it holds value 0; placing it in a row that already contains a given 0 VIOLATES the all-different constraint.

The classical predicate is f(x) = 1 if and only if decoding all free cells yields a completed grid that is a valid Latin square.
